clue.text: Hour thus employed, going in to watch fashionable programme

indicators.note: something fashionable can be fashioned, reshaped, so these letters are worked into a new order

parts.note: so means thus, in this way

explanation.surface: Someone spends an hour going round to watch a trendy television programme.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fashionable' looks like a description of the programme, but it signals the anagram of H, SO and WATCH; 'employed, going in to' only joins the pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: A talk show is a broadcast in which a host interviews guests, so it is a kind of programme.

clue.text: It's all come down to us in retreat with miles to go

definitions.text: It's all come down to us

indicators.note: to go means the named letter is removed and left out

parts.note: a hermitage is a secluded retreat, a hermit's dwelling

explanation.surface: Everything has come down to us in a hideaway still many miles away.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is a description: what has been handed down to us from the past.
explanation.definitionFit: Inheritance from earlier generations, traditions and buildings passed down, fits what has come down to us.

clue.text: Woman enters tricky heats in sports contest

indicators.note: enters means the word goes inside the rest
tricky signals that the letters of heats are rearranged into a less obvious order

parts.note: she is the pronoun for a woman

explanation.surface: A female athlete takes part in tough heats at a sporting event.
explanation.walkthrough: 'tricky' makes the anagram THEAS, and 'enters' places the woman before its final letter. The Ashes is the Test cricket series between England and Australia.
explanation.definitionFit: The Ashes is the long-running Test cricket series between England and Australia.

clue.text: Punch pirate captain

definitions.meaning: a boxer's short swinging blow with the elbow bent
the villain of Peter Pan who commands the pirate ship

explanation.definitionFit: A boxer's curving blow shares its name with the one-handed captain of Barrie's Peter Pan.

clue.text: Like bread to feast on: how soon, about?

indicators.note: about means the outer word goes round the inner one

parts.note: when asks how soon something will happen
to eat is to feast on food

explanation.surface: A diner asks how soon they can feast on some bread.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition calls for an adjective: bread made from a certain grain is so described.
explanation.definitionFit: Made of the grain used for most bread flour, so describing a loaf or its colour.

clue.text: War heroes of Wipers a doctor admitted

indicators.note: admitted means let in, so one word goes inside the other

parts.note: dusters are cloths used for wiping
MB, Bachelor of Medicine, is a doctor's qualification

explanation.surface: Wartime heroes of the Battle of Ypres are admitted by a doctor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wipers' was British soldiers' First World War name for Ypres, so the surface suggests that battle; here it is cloths. The Dambusters were the RAF squadron that breached German dams in 1943.
explanation.definitionFit: The 617 Squadron airmen who bombed the Ruhr dams in 1943 are celebrated as wartime heroes.

clue.text: Arrows he loosed from this?

indicators.note: loosed means set free, so the letters of arrows he are released into a new order

explanation.surface: A mounted archer shoots arrows from his horse.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is the definition too: a battle mount from which a medieval archer might shoot arrows.
explanation.definitionFit: A charger ridden into battle could be the platform from which an archer shoots.

clue.text: MFH may seek senior staff

definitions.meaning: Master of Foxhounds, the man or woman in charge of a fox hunt
to recruit executives by approaching people employed elsewhere

explanation.surface: A master of foxhounds might go looking for senior staff.
explanation.walkthrough: MFH is Master of Foxhounds, the leader of a British fox hunt: its head.
explanation.definitionFit: Executive recruiters poach top people; the master of a foxhunt leads it, so is head of it.

clue.text: Mercury's highly-visible period?

parts.note: not the planet or the god but the mercury in a thermometer, which climbs high and shows plainly during a spell of very hot weather

explanation.surface: An astronomer notes the time when the planet Mercury is easiest to see.
explanation.walkthrough: Mercury reads as the planet, best seen at certain times; it is really the liquid metal in a thermometer, standing high during a hot spell.
explanation.definitionFit: During a spell of unusually hot weather the thermometer's mercury column rises high and is easy to see.

clue.text: Got a bit bigger, say — revolting

indicators.note: say tells us the phrase is spoken and the spelling follows the sound

parts.note: grew some means got a bit bigger, increased somewhat

explanation.surface: Someone who has put on a little weight is told it looks disgusting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Got a bit bigger' is GREW SOME, which said aloud matches the answer's sound.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words describe something horrible or sickening to look at; they are synonyms.

clue.text: Taken by surprise, pronounce myself exhausted

parts.note: declaring something of oneself starts 'I am', so speaking of myself gives am
bushed is informal for exhausted, worn out

explanation.surface: Someone caught off guard declares that they are worn out.
explanation.walkthrough: To pronounce myself exhausted is to say 'I am bushed'; the AM and BUSHED run together.
explanation.definitionFit: To be caught in a surprise attack by people lying in wait is to be taken by surprise.

clue.text: Priest's taking in boy orphan

indicators.note: taking in means one word swallows the other, holding it inside

parts.note: Father is the title of a Catholic priest, and the possessive gives the S
Les is a boy's name, short for Leslie

explanation.surface: A priest takes an orphaned boy into his care.
explanation.walkthrough: 'orphan' is used as an adjective here, describing a child who has lost a parent.
explanation.definitionFit: An orphan child has lost a parent, and one without a male parent is in that position.

clue.text: Some holes to birdie in tournament

parts.note: a round of golf covers a set of holes, usually eighteen
a robin is a small bird, a birdie

explanation.surface: A golfer hopes to score birdies on some holes during a competition.
explanation.walkthrough: 'birdie' suggests golf's one under par, but it is a small bird.
explanation.definitionFit: A competition in which every player meets every other in turn is this kind of tournament.

clue.text: From amateur, dull speech

indicators.note: From tells us the letters are taken out of the run of words amateur dull

explanation.surface: A dull talk given by an amateur speaker.
explanation.walkthrough: 'speech' reads as an address, but it means a language.
explanation.definitionFit: Speech can mean a language or tongue, and this is one spoken in Pakistan and India.

clue.text: With new university place, carefully studies Greek hero

indicators.note: new together with place says one letter is shifted to a fresh position in the word
place, after new, completes the instruction to put the letter somewhere else

parts.note: peruses means reads or studies carefully

explanation.surface: A scholar takes up a post at a new university and studies a Greek hero carefully.
explanation.walkthrough: Take PERUSES and move its U, the university, two places later to get the hero's name.
explanation.definitionFit: Son of Zeus who slew Medusa, the Gorgon, and rescued Andromeda: a hero of Greek myth.

clue.text: Glow, contributing 99% of genius?

definitions.meaning: a genteel euphemism for sweating, as in 'horses sweat, men sweat, ladies glow'
Edison said genius is one per cent inspiration and ninety-nine per cent sweat

explanation.surface: A radiant face shows the hard work behind brilliance.
explanation.walkthrough: Edison's saying holds that genius is 1% inspiration and 99% perspiration, so sweating supplies the 99%.
explanation.definitionFit: To sweat is politely to glow, and Edison credited sweat with 99 per cent of genius.

clue.text: Arrested for slashing tyres

indicators.note: slashing cuts the word arrested up so the pieces can be rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone is arrested for slashing car tyres.
explanation.walkthrough: 'slashing' reads as the crime but signals the anagram; retreads are tyres given new treads.
explanation.definitionFit: Retreads are old tyres with fresh rubber treads moulded on.

clue.text: In fall, knock computer key in

indicators.note: the second in places one word within another

parts.note: a dent is the mark a knock leaves, and to dent is to knock
Esc, escape, is a key on a computer keyboard

explanation.surface: In autumn someone thumps a key on their computer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fall' reads as autumn, with 'In fall' a time phrase; the first 'In' is a link and 'fall' is a drop.
explanation.definitionFit: A going down or drop from a height is a fall.

clue.text: Row about deanery gradually got nearer

parts.note: a cathedral close is the precinct where the deanery stands
a din is a row, a loud noise

explanation.surface: An argument about the dean's residence slowly drew closer.
explanation.walkthrough: A close is the enclosed grounds of a cathedral, housing the deanery; 'Row' is noise, not a quarrel.
explanation.definitionFit: To advance on, surround and draw nearer step by step, as fog or enemies do.

clue.text: Swiftly drop nameless salad plant boy originally picked up

indicators.note: originally means the reversed boy goes at the very start
picked up, in a down clue, means the word is lifted and read upwards

parts.note: a son is a boy

indicators.note: nameless means the letter N, for name, is dropped

parts.note: endive is a salad plant like chicory

explanation.surface: A boy hastily drops a salad plant and then picks it up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'picked up' turns SON into NOS, and 'originally' puts it first; 'nameless' takes N from ENDIVE, leaving EDIVE.
explanation.definitionFit: A steep headlong plunge, as by an aircraft or share prices, is a swift drop.

clue.text: Grant for novel

definitions.meaning: the first name of ... S. Grant, US Civil War general and president
James Joyce's 1922 novel set in Dublin

explanation.surface: Someone receives funding to write a novel.
explanation.definitionFit: General Grant's first name is also the title of Joyce's famous novel.

clue.text: Badger-like creature's lost a little speed

indicators.note: lost a little says the word loses a small bit from its end, its last letter

parts.note: the ratel is the honey badger of Africa and Asia

explanation.surface: A badger-like animal has slowed down a little.
explanation.walkthrough: The ratel, or honey badger, may be unfamiliar; drop its final L.
explanation.definitionFit: Rate can mean pace or velocity, as in moving at a fast rate.

clue.text: Boar's Head at Eastcheap, say, a subject for drama?

definitions.meaning: the tavern in Shakespeare's Henry IV haunted by Doll Tearsheet, so her home ground
the title of Ibsen's play about Nora and her marriage

explanation.surface: Shakespeare's tavern in Eastcheap might make a good topic for a play.
explanation.walkthrough: In Henry IV the Boar's Head tavern in Eastcheap is where Doll Tearsheet plies her trade, making it Doll's house; Ibsen's play takes the same title.
explanation.definitionFit: A tavern frequented by the character Doll is her house, and the phrase is also an Ibsen play title.

clue.text: Apparently virtuous vicar arrested — his record?

indicators.note: arrested means held, so one word takes the other into custody inside it

parts.note: pious means devout or righteous, outwardly virtuous
Rev, short for Reverend, is the title of a vicar

explanation.surface: A seemingly good vicar is arrested, raising the question of his criminal history.
explanation.walkthrough: In British police slang a suspect 'has previous', meaning past convictions; that is the noun defined by 'his record'.
explanation.definitionFit: British slang for a criminal history, earlier convictions on file.

clue.text: Think island warm

definitions.meaning: an island of the Inner Hebrides off western Scotland
to heat wine or ale with spices

explanation.surface: Imagine a warm island.
explanation.definitionFit: To ponder, a Hebridean island and to heat spiced wine share one word.

clue.text: Private second to be killed protecting square

indicators.note: protecting means the outer letters surround and shield the inner word

parts.note: to die is to be killed
a quad, quadrangle, is a square courtyard as in a college

explanation.surface: A private soldier is the next to die while guarding the parade square.
explanation.walkthrough: A squaddie is British slang for a private soldier; 'Private' reads as an adjective but is the rank.
explanation.definitionFit: Informal British word for a private, the lowest rank of soldier in the army.

clue.text: Old counsel needs brandy, having to change terms

parts.note: rede is an archaic word for advice or counsel
fine is a French brandy of good quality, as in fine champagne

explanation.surface: A lawyer from the old school needs a brandy and must renegotiate a contract.
explanation.walkthrough: 'counsel' suggests a barrister, but REDE is the old word for advice; FINE is brandy.
explanation.definitionFit: To set out the meanings of words afresh is to alter the terms in which something is framed.

clue.text: Relaxing, reclines in part of car

indicators.note: relaxing loosens the word reclines so its letters can settle into a new order

explanation.surface: A passenger relaxes by reclining in the car seat.
explanation.walkthrough: A silencer is the British term for a car's muffler, part of the exhaust system.
explanation.definitionFit: A device in the exhaust system of a car that reduces engine noise, the US muffler.
